Consider the vector field [MATH: \mathbf F,] given by

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf F(x,y)= P(x,y)\,\mathbf{i} + Q(x,y)\,\mathbf{j}]

Content:
which is defined on an open set [MATH: D\subseteq \mathbb R^2.] Recall that a function [MATH: \psi(x,y)] is said to be a stream function of [MATH: \mathbf F] if it satisfies

Content:
[MATH: P = \dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial y}, \qquad
Q = -\dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial x}.]

Content:
If a vector field [MATH: \mathbf{F}(x,y)] has a stream function [MATH: \psi(x,y),] then [MATH: \mathbf{F}] is called a source-free vector field.

Content:
Source-free vector fields have some interesting properties, summarized below:

Content:
- The divergence of [MATH: \mathbf{F}] at any point of [MATH: D] is zero:
[MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf{F} = \nabla \cdot \mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = 0]
- The flux of [MATH: \mathbf{F}] along any closed curve [MATH: C \in D] is zero:
[MATH: \oint\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s = 0]
- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves [MATH: C_1, C_2 \in D] with the same start and endpoints, we have that
[MATH: \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s.]

Stream functions for source-free vector fields play a similar role to potential functions for conservative vector fields. So it's worth comparing them side-by-side.

items.title: Identifying True Statements Regarding Source-Free Vector Fields

sections.normalized_html:
Given the vector field [MATH: \mathbf{F}(x,y) = 4y(x^2+y^2)\,\mathbf{i} - 4x(x^2+y^2)\,\mathbf{j},] which of the following statements must be true?

  1. [MATH: \nabla \cdot \mathbf F= 0]

  2. [MATH: \mathbf{F}] is a source-free vector field

  3. For two arbitrary curves [MATH: C_1] and [MATH: C_2,] we have [MATH: \displaystyle\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s \neq \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s.]
sections.readable_text:
Given the vector field [MATH: \mathbf{F}(x,y) = 4y(x^2+y^2)\,\mathbf{i} - 4x(x^2+y^2)\,\mathbf{j},] which of the following statements must be true?

1. [MATH: \nabla \cdot \mathbf F= 0]
2. [MATH: \mathbf{F}] is a source-free vector field
3. For two arbitrary curves [MATH: C_1] and [MATH: C_2,] we have [MATH: \displaystyle\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s \neq \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
If [MATH: \mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf{i} + Q\,\mathbf{j}] is a vector field with simply connected domain [MATH: D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2,] then the following are equivalent:

  • [MATH: \mathbf{F}] is a source-free vector field.

  • [MATH: \nabla \cdot \mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = 0.]

  • The flux [MATH: \displaystyle{\oint\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s}] along any closed curve [MATH: C \in D] is zero.

  • Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves [MATH: C_1,C_2 \in D] with the same start and endpoints, we have that [MATH: \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s.]

  • There exists a stream function [MATH: \psi(x,y)] for [MATH: \mathbf{F}.]

Note that [MATH: \mathbf{F}(x,y)] is a vector field with the simply connected domain [MATH: D=\mathbb{R}^2,] where

[MATH: P(x,y) = 4y(x^2+y^2),\qquad Q(x,y) = - 4x(x^2+y^2).]

Computing the partial derivatives, we have

[MATH: (∂P)/(∂x) = 8xy, (∂Q)/(∂y)|= − 8xy.]

With that in mind, let's consider each statement.

  • Statement I is true. Indeed, we have that [MATH: \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = 8xy + (-8xy) = 0.]

  • Statement II is true. This follows from statement I.

  • Statement III is false. Since [MATH: \mathbf F] is source-free, we have that [MATH: \displaystyle\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s] for all curves with the same start and endpoints.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

The curve [MATH: C_1] has endpoints [MATH: A(5,3)] and [MATH: B(1,3).] Calculate the flux of the vector field
[MATH: \mathbf{F}(x,y)=\sqrt{y^3}\,\mathbf{i}+\sqrt{(5-x)^3}\,\mathbf{j}]
through [MATH: C_1] measured with respect to the unit normal vector [MATH: \mathbf{n}_1,] as shown above.

Hint: You're given that [MATH: \mathbf F] is source-free.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
If [MATH: \mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf{i} + Q\,\mathbf{j}] is a vector field with simply connected domain [MATH: D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2,] then the following are equivalent:

  • [MATH: \mathbf{F}] is a source-free vector field.

  • [MATH: \nabla \cdot \mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = 0.]

  • The flux [MATH: \displaystyle{\oint\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s}] along any closed curve [MATH: C \in D] is zero.

  • Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves [MATH: C_1, C_2 \in D] with the same start and endpoints, we have that [MATH: \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s.]

  • There exists a stream function [MATH: \psi(x,y)] for [MATH: \mathbf{F}.]

First, notice that

[MATH: \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\sqrt{y^3}\right) + \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(\sqrt{(5-x)^3}\right) = 0+0 = 0,]

which shows that [MATH: \mathbf{F}] is a source-free vector field.

Since [MATH: \mathbf{F}] is source-free, we know the flux of [MATH: \mathbf{F}] is independent of the path. In particular,

[MATH: \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \,\textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \,\textrm{d}s,]

where [MATH: C_2] is the straight line from [MATH: A(5,3)] to [MATH: B(1,3)] and [MATH: \mathbf{n}_2] is its unit normal, shown in the diagram below.

Notice that both [MATH: \mathbf n_1] and [MATH: \mathbf n_2] are [MATH: 90^\circ] clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

To calculate the flux of [MATH: \mathbf F] across [MATH: C_2,] we will use the formula

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Consider the vector field [MATH: \mathbf F,] given by

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf F(x,y)= P(x,y)\,\mathbf{i} + Q(x,y)\,\mathbf{j}]

Content:
which is defined on an open set [MATH: D\subseteq \mathbb R^2.] Recall that a function [MATH: \psi(x,y)] is said to be a stream function of [MATH: \mathbf F] if it satisfies

Content:
[MATH: P = \dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial y}, \qquad
Q = -\dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial x}.]

Content:
If a vector field [MATH: \mathbf{F}(x,y)] has a stream function [MATH: \psi(x,y),] then [MATH: \mathbf{F}] is called a source-free vector field.

Content:
Source-free vector fields have some interesting properties, summarized below:

Content:
- The divergence of [MATH: \mathbf{F}] at any point of [MATH: D] is zero:
[MATH: \textrm{div}\,\mathbf{F} = \nabla \cdot \mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = 0]
- The flux of [MATH: \mathbf{F}] along any closed curve [MATH: C \in D] is zero:
[MATH: \oint\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s = 0]
- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves [MATH: C_1, C_2 \in D] with the same start and endpoints, we have that
[MATH: \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s.]

Content:
Stream functions for source-free vector fields play a similar role to potential functions for conservative vector fields. So it's worth comparing them side-by-side.

Content:
| | Source-Free | / | Stream Function [MATH: \psi] | [MATH: \mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial y}\,\mathbf i - \dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial x}\,\mathbf j] | / | Relationship between [MATH: \psi] and [MATH: \mathbf F] | [MATH: \mathbf F] is tangential to [MATH: \psi]'s level curves | / | Divergence is zero | [MATH: \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = 0] | / | Flux is zero along closed curves | [MATH: \displaystyle\oint\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s = 0] | / | Flux integrals are path independent | [MATH: \displaystyle\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s] | | | | Conservative | / | Potential Function [MATH: \phi] | [MATH: \mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial \phi}{\partial x}\,\mathbf i + \dfrac{\partial \phi}{\partial y}\,\mathbf j] | / | Relationship between [MATH: \phi] and [MATH: \mathbf F] | [MATH: \mathbf F] is perpendicular to [MATH: \phi]'s level curves | / | (Scalar) curl is zero | [MATH: \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 0] | / | Circulation is zero along closed curves | [MATH: \displaystyle\oint\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm d \mathbf{r}= 0] | / | Line integrals are path independent | [MATH: \displaystyle\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm d \mathbf{r} = \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F}\cdot \textrm d \mathbf{r}] | |

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: A Worked Example

Content:
Let's use what we know about source-free vector fields to calculate the flux of

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{F}(x,y)=2y\,\mathbf{i}-2x\,\mathbf{j}]

Content:
across the curve [MATH: C,] shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/201ea211d60d0c1ad5562d6680badb3e]

Content:
First, notice that this is a source-free vector field, since

Content:
[MATH: (∂P)/(∂x) + (∂Q)/(∂y)|= (∂)/(∂x)(2y) + (∂)/(∂y)(− 2x); = 0 + 0; = 0.]

Content:
Therefore, since [MATH: \mathbf{F}] is source-free, the flux of [MATH: \mathbf{F}] across any closed curve is zero. Hence,

Content:
[MATH: \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s
=
0.]

Item 3 — Example: Identifying True Statements Regarding Source-Free Vector Fields

Example Prompt:
Given the vector field [MATH: \mathbf{F}(x,y) = 4y(x^2+y^2)\,\mathbf{i} - 4x(x^2+y^2)\,\mathbf{j},] which of the following statements must be true?

1. [MATH: \nabla \cdot \mathbf F= 0]
2. [MATH: \mathbf{F}] is a source-free vector field
3. For two arbitrary curves [MATH: C_1] and [MATH: C_2,] we have [MATH: \displaystyle\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s \neq \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
If [MATH: \mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf{i} + Q\,\mathbf{j}] is a vector field with simply connected domain [MATH: D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2,] then the following are equivalent:

- [MATH: \nabla \cdot \mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = 0.]
- The flux [MATH: \displaystyle{\oint\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s}] along any closed curve [MATH: C \in D] is zero.
- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves [MATH: C_1,C_2 \in D] with the same start and endpoints, we have that
[MATH: \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s.]
- There exists a stream function [MATH: \psi(x,y)] for [MATH: \mathbf{F}.]

Note that [MATH: \mathbf{F}(x,y)] is a vector field with the simply connected domain [MATH: D=\mathbb{R}^2,] where

[MATH: P(x,y) = 4y(x^2+y^2),\qquad Q(x,y) = - 4x(x^2+y^2).]

Computing the partial derivatives, we have

[MATH: (∂P)/(∂x) = 8xy, (∂Q)/(∂y)|= − 8xy.]

With that in mind, let's consider each statement.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, we have that
[MATH: \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y}
=
8xy + (-8xy) = 0.]
- Statement II is true. This follows from statement I.
- Statement III is false. Since [MATH: \mathbf F] is source-free, we have that [MATH: \displaystyle\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}s] for all curves with the same start and endpoints.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."
